How money is earned and spent

Every change to the player's money in every run, tagged by where it came from. Clearing an encounter pays $10, plus $2 per unused grid and $5 for a boss. On top of that come currency tiles, pink tiles (saved in the piggy bank during scoring, then paid back double at the start of the next stage), sticker and stamp effects, Dragon interest and selling items. Money goes on stickers, stamps, restocks and tiles, and some bosses and items take money.

Stickers and stamps

“Buy rate” is how often the AI bought an item when it was in the shop and affordable. “Win lift” compares the runs that held the item at stage 3 with runs at the same crown that didn't, so an item the AI mostly holds at easy crowns doesn't look good just for that. The grey whisker is ±1 standard error, and a lift whose whisker crosses zero could be chance.

What stands out

  1. Crown 7 is a cliff. Wins fall from — at crown 6 to — at crown 7, the crown where each encounter gives 4 grids instead of 5.
  2. High-crown runs die early, not at the end. Most losses happen on stages 3 and 4, and the stage-3 boss alone takes about one loss in six. Runs that reach the final boss win about 92% of the time.
  3. Characters spread apart as crowns rise. Octacles and Cretaceous Meg hold up at crowns 6–7. Rodman, Nina Nix, Sandy Saguaro and Human Boy lose 35–44 points between crowns 0–3 and crowns 4–7.
  4. Amphora is the strongest win marker: holding it at stage 3 is worth — points after adjusting for crown. Next come Oden at —, Haunted House at — and Cursed VHS at —.
  5. The worst markers are Wheezy Vixen at —, Dartboard at — and Chick at —. Many of these shrink by about half once character is taken into account, so part of the gap is which characters buy them.
  6. Moai is the clearest overbuy. The AI buys it — of the time it can afford it, yet runs holding it do — points worse, and it is often sold later.
  7. The AI buys from a narrow core. The top 10 items take about two-thirds of all buys, and 187 of 273 items are bought less than 2% of the time. Dragon is never bought.
  8. Money mostly comes from clearing encounters. Per run that is —, plus — for unused grids and — from bosses. Sticker and stamp effects add —, almost all from Jack-o'-Lantern. Currency tiles add — and selling items adds —.
  9. Money goes to stickers (— per run), stamps (—) and restocks (—). Nearly half of restock streaks end without a buy.
  10. At high crowns the AI often skips Michael. When it does take him on at crown 7, it wins about three times in four.
  11. Worth checking in the real game: Michael never appears at crown 0, Coin Purse costs $3 per grid and pays almost nothing back, and Dragon is never worth buying. Any of these could be a simulator quirk.

How these numbers were made, and definitions
Runs
Simulated full runs in the solver's port of the game: 11 characters × 8 crowns × 24 seeds. The seeds are fresh (not used in training). Each character plays with the current target plan (Curse for Sam Gambit at crowns 3–7, otherwise free).
The AI
The live assistant's policy network, picking its top choice at every step. The real assistant also searches a few moves ahead, which this skips for speed, so these win rates are a little lower than the assistant gives in play.
Won
Beat the final boss at stage 5. Beating Michael afterwards is optional. Losing to him still counts as a win.
Buy rate
Times bought ÷ times the item sat in a shop while the AI could afford it. Every restock counts as a new appearance.
Win lift
For each crown, the win rate of runs holding the item at the start of stage 3 minus that of the runs that reached stage 3 without it, averaged with weights by how many held it. It shows association, not cause: an item can look good because the AI buys it in runs that were already going well.
Money
Every change to the player's money is tagged where the game makes it: encounter clear rewards ($10, +$2 per unused grid, +$5 at a boss, Dragon interest), scoring steps (currency tiles, pink tiles, each sticker's or stamp's money effect, money the Fox boss steals), grid-start item effects (such as Golden Scales, Takeout Box, Coin Purse), the piggy-bank payout at the start of a stage, sells, buys, restocks, tiles and Wheel rerolls. Per run, the tagged changes add up exactly to the money the run ends with. Pink tiles move money into the piggy bank, which pays them back doubled, so a pink tile's net gain is the payout minus the saving.
Not included
Tile (consumable) choices, the order items sit in, and word-by-word play are not broken out here. The trace records them only as totals.
